title: Hyperbole & Onomatopoeia: Exaggeration & Sound Effects
description: Lesson 5 in the Fables Figurative Language series. Discover how authors make fables louder and sillier with extreme exaggeration (hyperbole) and sound-effect words (onomatopoeia) — building on similes, personification, and metaphors.
author: Damilare Adeyemi Adepoju

props.title: Story So Far
props.content: You already explored similes (like/as), personification, and metaphors. Today fable writers turn the volume up — with exaggeration and sound-effect words that make beasts fight, boast, and buzz!

Your Mission Today

You will learn two new tools: hyperbole (extreme exaggeration) and onomatopoeia (words that copy real sounds). By the end, you will spot both inside a fable and know why writers use them.

props.question: Before we learn the fancy names — which sentence sounds the silliest to you?

options.text: I've told you a million times!
I could eat an entire mountain of apples!
This bag weighs a thousand tonnes!
I waited for a hundred years!

items.title: What is hyperbole in one sentence?
items.content: Hyperbole is when a writer stretches the truth to an impossible extreme — like saying 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse!'

items.title: How do I spot onomatopoeia?
items.content: Say the word out loud! If it sounds like the noise it describes — CRACK, SPLASH, BZZZZ — it's onomatopoeia.

items.title: Why do fable writers use both?
items.content: Hyperbole shows how strongly a character feels. Onomatopoeia lets the reader HEAR the action. Together they make fables exciting!

props.content:
Two New Tools

Hyperbole stretches the truth on purpose — nobody believes it literally. Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like the noise it names, such as BUZZ or CRASH.

cards.back: Extreme exaggeration for emphasis or humour — NOT meant literally.
A word that imitates a real sound, like BUZZ or CRASH.
Making something sound bigger, faster, or more extreme than it really is.
A word written to be heard — often in CAPITALS with an exclamation mark!

props.statement: Hyperbole and onomatopoeia are meant to be taken completely literally.
props.explanation: Hyperbole stretches the truth on purpose — nobody really waits a million years! Onomatopoeia is a sound word like BOOM!, not a plain fact.

props.alt: A boastful hare and a proud lion — fable characters used to show extreme exaggeration
props.caption: Hyperbole makes feelings LOUDER than life!

props.content:
Spotting Hyperbole

Hyperbole shows how strongly a character feels by stretching the truth far beyond what is possible. A boastful hare claiming he can run 'faster than light' highlights his arrogance — no one actually believes it, and that's the point.

props.title: Match Each Example to Its Device

props.statement: 'The Lion roared so loudly that the earth split in half' is an example of hyperbole.
props.explanation: No roar can literally split the earth — this is an extreme exaggeration to show how loud and angry the Lion is.

questions.question: Why does a writer use hyperbole?

options.text: To trick the reader into believing something false
To emphasise a feeling with dramatic, humorous exaggeration
Because they don't know the real facts

questions.explanation: Hyperbole is used deliberately for emphasis or humour — everyone knows it isn't literally true.

props.alt: A tree branch snapping under a bear's weight, with the word CRACK bursting from the branch
props.caption: CRACK! — say it out loud. Does it sound like a branch breaking?

props.content:
The Golden Rule

An onomatopoeia word imitates the actual sound of the thing it describes. Say the word out loud — if it sounds like the noise it's naming (like CRACK, BUZZ, or SPLASH), it's onomatopoeia!

hotspots.content: Hyperbole: 'The Lion roared so loudly that the earth split in half.' (Extreme exaggeration of volume).

props.content:
Detective Debrief

Great work! You found onomatopoeia in the buzzing and claw sounds, and hyperbole in the impossible roar and thousand swipes. Fable writers mix both to make action feel huge and loud.

props.title: Complete the Fable Sentence
props.text: The thirsty Crow felt as if he hadn't drunk water in a million {{blank}}.

items.title: Step 1 — Start with a true feeling
items.content: Begin with something real: 'I am very tired' or 'I am very hungry.'

items.title: Step 2 — Pick a number, size, or speed
items.content: Choose something connected to the feeling — years, mountains, or lightning speed.

items.title: Step 3 — Push it to an impossible extreme
items.content: 'I'm tired' becomes 'I could sleep for a hundred years!' Nobody believes it literally — that's the joke.

items.title: Step 4 — Add a sound word
items.content: Pair hyperbole with onomatopoeia for extra drama — like YAWN! or CRASH!

props.title: Put the Hyperbole Steps in Order

items.text: Start with a true feeling (e.g. I am very tired)
Pick a number, size, or speed connected to it
Push it to an impossible extreme (e.g. a hundred years)
Say it confidently, as if it were completely true!

questions.question: 'CRASH! went the falling tree' — hyperbole or onomatopoeia?
questions.explanation: CRASH! imitates the sound of the tree falling — that's onomatopoeia.
